workload.row_markup: {id}{label}
workload.determinism_note: Upstream draws labels with Math.random(). This harness uses a fixed-seed xorshift32 instead, and every arm consumes the identical sequence, so all arms build a byte-identical tree. Without that the arms would not be comparable at all: different text is a different number of bytes across the boundary. xorshift32 specifically, because it is 32-bit and JavaScript can therefore execute it exactly. Upstream's biased `% max` fold is kept so the label distribution still matches upstream's.

crossover.headline: Interning pays above a repetition ratio of R = 36 for short names, 54 for long names (R = total name uses / distinct names). Below it the native binding is slower than the JavaScript one on the same tree.
crossover.machine_independent: Needing no exchange rate and true on every machine: an interned tier costs one extra boundary crossing per distinct name and saves (uses - distinct) x mean-name-length bytes. At a repetition ratio of exactly 1 it copies the same bytes as a non-interning binding and adds one crossing per name, so it strictly loses. Each configuration's break-even figure is the bytes it saves per crossing it spends: interning pays there if and only if a crossing is cheaper than that many bytes.
crossover.interpretation: The two estimates disagree for long names, and the gap is the point. The contrast model says the atom tier already pays from R = 3, but the native path does not overtake JavaScript until R = 54. Interning is therefore not what loses in between: the rest of the path is, and on this harness that means wasmi interpreting the guest. A compiled guest would move the observed crossover down toward the modelled one without changing the ABI at all.

observed.explanation: The native binding wins at a repetition ratio of 39.5 (v150-short-many-real at 1.01x) and loses at 19.9 (v300-short-many-real at 0.90x). Interpolating in log-ratio puts the crossing at R = 36.
The native binding wins at a repetition ratio of 73.2 (v80-long-many-real at 1.05x) and loses at 39.5 (v150-long-many-real at 0.95x). Interpolating in log-ratio puts the crossing at R = 54.

contrasts.caveat: From 2 crossing pairs and 7 byte pairs, each differing in exactly one axis. Machine-local: k is a property of this chip and build, not of the ABI.

thresholds.explanation: At 3 bytes per name and k = 148 bytes per crossing, interning pays above R = 45.
At 70 bytes per name and k = 148 bytes per crossing, interning pays above R = 3.

arms.description: JS over the existing script runtime (Boa), against the engine's DOM

notes: 10000 strings crossed from the JavaScript heap, none of them interned: a tag or attribute name is copied again on every call that uses it.
Per-operation `bytes_copied` is reported as 0 because the byte counter sits at the single string-conversion point rather than in each binding. The arm total is exact.
`process_allocations` includes Boa's own work for this call, not only the DOM bindings. It is the cost of running the workload in this arm, not an attribution to the boundary alone.

arms.description: wasm-bindgen, default (interning off)

notes: Confirmed against emitted glue (wasm-bindgen-cli 0.2.127, web-sys 0.3.104, --target web, a probe crate issuing the same five operations): each shim decodes its string arguments with getStringFromWasm0 and performs exactly one DOM interaction, and no object-reclamation intrinsic is emitted. Not confirmed: the interned configuration, because the probe was built without `enable-interning`. Its byte figure is still read from cache/intern.rs, and it is the figure that favours wasm-bindgen.

Model read from: web-sys-0.3.104/src/features/gen_Document.rs (create_element, create_text_node); web-sys-0.3.104/src/features/gen_Node.rs (append_child, set_text_content); web-sys-0.3.104/src/features/gen_Element.rs (set_attribute); wasm-bindgen-0.2.127/src/{lib.rs,convert/slices.rs,cache/intern.rs}; glue emitted by wasm-bindgen-cli 0.2.127 --target web for a probe crate calling the same five operations.

12000 guest-to-shim transitions and 12000 shim-to-DOM transitions, two per operation. The second of each pair is the call arm A makes directly, so the glue's contribution is the first: 12000 transitions that exist only because a JavaScript intermediary is in the path.

Returned DOM objects cross as externrefs and cost no crossing to release: emitted glue contains no `__wbindgen_object_drop_ref`, `addHeapObject`, `takeObject` or `getObject`. An earlier version of this model charged 20,000 reclamation crossings on `create-1000`, which is the pre-reference-types ABI and no longer what the toolchain generates.
`process_allocations` is 0 because nothing ran, and `binding_reported_allocations` is absent because with externrefs there is no JS-side object table whose occupancy could be reported.
This is the out-of-the-box configuration. `enable-interning` is a non-default feature, so a guest that does nothing special pays these numbers.

Bytes are UTF-8, to stay comparable with arms A and C. wasm-bindgen's own documentation notes the copy also re-encodes UTF-8 to UTF-16, so the bytes written on the JavaScript side are up to twice these.

unmeasured_axes.why_it_matters: This is the most likely weakness in the whole design. Every write in the ABI moves handles and atoms and copies nothing, but a read has to get data back into guest memory, and the facade's readers return owned `String`s. A read is therefore expected to cost two copies: one into the host's `String` and one into the guest's linear memory. A page that reads as much as it writes could erase the entire interning advantage, and nothing here would show it.
unmeasured_axes.what_blocks_it: The ABI has no read operations at all. There is nothing to call, so there is nothing to count, and a model of a read would be a guess about an implementation nobody has written.
operations_required: get_bounding_client_rect(node) -> geometry (also needs a layout flush, which the facade does not do)
unmeasured_axes.expected_finding: Two copies per read against wasm-bindgen's one, which would make reads the axis where the native binding loses outright. An atom-returning `get_attribute` would avoid it for the interned tier; text and geometry could not.

unmeasured_axes.why_it_matters: Handles are never reused and never freed, by design: a detached node stays addressable, so a handle to it stays meaningful. That is the right trade for a page that grows and the wrong one for a list that churns. A create/destroy/reorder cycle would grow the handle table without bound, and nothing currently measures that.
unmeasured_axes.what_blocks_it: There is no `remove` and no `insert_before`, so a create/destroy/reorder cycle cannot be expressed. `append_child` detaches from the previous parent, which permits a move but not a removal and not an ordered insertion.
operations_required: a generational handle, so a freed slot can be reused without a stale handle silently addressing a new node
unmeasured_axes.expected_finding: Handle-table growth proportional to total nodes ever created rather than nodes alive, and a swap-rows workload that costs a long-lived page more the longer it runs. wasm-bindgen's heap slots are freed on drop, so it has no equivalent leak.

reading_notes: The point of the sweep is to find where the native binding LOSES. If it appears to win everywhere, treat that as evidence the axes are too narrow or the benchmark is broken, not that the ABI is perfect.
`crossover.worst_for_native` is reported as prominently as the best case, on purpose. Read it first.

The crossover ratio R is machine-local, because it depends on an exchange rate between a crossing and a byte that has to be measured. `crossover.machine_independent` states the half of the trade that needs no exchange rate and holds everywhere.

Two axes are named in `unmeasured_axes` and cannot be run: read-heavy workloads and structural churn. Both are places this design is most likely to lose. They are absent from the numbers, not from the analysis.
Counts are the result. They are properties of the interface and are identical on every machine that runs this workload.
Timings are secondary, are valid only against each other within this one run on this one machine, and must never be compared across machines or sessions.
Arm B was not run. Every arm-B number is statically derived from web-sys signatures and wasm-bindgen's ABI, is marked `"derivation": "static_analysis"`, and has no timing.
Arm B is reported in two configurations because wasm-bindgen's string interning is a non-default cargo feature. Comparing only against the default would be comparing against interning switched off.

`bytes_copied_steady_state` excludes the cost of learning a page's vocabulary. Read it together with `bytes_copied`: the first is what a running application pays per mutation, the second is what the first paint pays including the learning.

`process_allocations` is taken from a global allocator below every crate involved, so it includes the language runtime, not only the binding. Where an arm also reports `binding_reported_allocations`, the gap between them is what that binding cannot see.
